**Answer: Yes — every positive real number can be expressed as the sum of a subsequence.**

---

### Proof

We prove that for any $x>0$ there exists a subsequence $(a_{n_k})_{k\ge 1}$ with $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ such that $\sum_{k\ge 1} a_{n_k}=x$. The tool is a greedy algorithm; the hypotheses $a_i\to 0$ and $\sum a_i=\infty$ are exactly what force its remainder to vanish.

**Greedy construction.** Set $r_0=x$ and $n_0=0$. Having chosen $n_0<n_1<\cdots<n_{k-1}$ with $r_{k-1}>0$, define $n_k$ to be the **smallest** index $i>n_{k-1}$ with $a_i\le r_{k-1}$, and set
$$r_k \;=\; r_{k-1}-a_{n_k}.$$

Such an $n_k$ always exists: since $a_i\to 0$, eventually $a_i<r_{k-1}$, so some $i>n_{k-1}$ satisfies $a_i\le r_{k-1}$. By construction $r_k\ge 0$ for all $k$. Because $(a_i)$ is strictly decreasing, "smallest index with $a_i\le r_{k-1}$" is the same as "largest term $\le r_{k-1}$ among the remaining terms."

**The remainder tends to $0$.** The sequence $(r_k)$ is non-increasing and bounded below by $0$, so $r_k\to L$ for some $L\ge 0$. We claim $L=0$.

Suppose for contradiction that $L>0$. Pick $K_0$ and $M$ so that

* $r_k\ge L/2$ for all $k\ge K_0$, and
* $a_i < L/2$ for all $i\ge M$.

Enlarge $K_0$ if necessary so that $n_{K_0}\ge M$ (possible since $n_k\to\infty$). Then for every $k\ge K_0$ we have $n_k\ge M$, hence
$$a_{n_k+1} \;<\; L/2 \;\le\; r_k.$$
So $a_{n_k+1}$ is eligible (it is $\le r_k$ and has index $>n_k$), and it is the **largest** eligible term because the sequence is strictly decreasing. Therefore the greedy rule selects it:
$$n_{k+1}=n_k+1,\qquad r_{k+1}=r_k-a_{n_k+1}.$$

Iterating from $K_0$ to any $K>K_0$,
$$r_K \;=\; r_{K_0}-\sum_{j=K_0}^{K-1} a_{n_j+1} \;=\; r_{K_0}-\sum_{i\,=\,n_{K_0}+1}^{\,n_{K}+1} a_i.$$
As $K\to\infty$ the index $n_K\to\infty$, so the sum on the right tends to $\sum_{i=n_{K_0}+1}^{\infty}a_i$, which is $+\infty$ because $\sum a_i=\infty$ (a tail of a divergent series of positive terms diverges). Thus $r_K\to -\infty$, contradicting $r_K\ge L/2>0$.

Hence $L=0$.

**Conclusion.** Since $r_k\to 0$ and $r_k=x-\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{n_j}$, we obtain
$$x \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_{n_k},$$
a subsequence sum. The argument uses only $a_i\to 0$, $\sum a_i=\infty$, and strict decrease (the last only to make "largest eligible term" unambiguous), so it applies to **every** sequence satisfying the hypotheses. Therefore every positive real number is representable as a subsequence sum. $\blacksquare$

$$r_k \;=\; r_{k-1}-a_{n_k}.$$

Such an $n_k$ always exists: since $a_i\to 0$, eventually $a_i<r_{k-1}$, so some $i>n_{k-1}$ satisfies $a_i\le r_{k-1}$. By construction $r_k\ge 0$ for all $k$. Because $(a_i)$ is strictly decreasing, "smallest index with $a_i\le r_{k-1}$" is the same as "largest term $\le r_{k-1}$ among the remaining terms."

**The remainder tends to $0$.** The sequence $(r_k)$ is non-increasing and bounded below by $0$, so $r_k\to L$ for some $L\ge 0$. We claim $L=0$.

Suppose for contradiction that $L>0$. Pick $K_0$ and $M$ so that

* $r_k\ge L/2$ for all $k\ge K_0$, and
* $a_i < L/2$ for all $i\ge M$.

Enlarge $K_0$ if necessary so that $n_{K_0}\ge M$ (possible since $n_k\to\infty$). Then for every $k\ge K_0$ we have $n_k\ge M$, hence
$$a_{n_k+1} \;<\; L/2 \;\le\; r_k.$$
So $a_{n_k+1}$ is eligible (it is $\le r_k$ and has index $>n_k$), and it is the **largest** eligible term because the sequence is strictly decreasing. Therefore the greedy rule selects it:
$$n_{k+1}=n_k+1,\qquad r_{k+1}=r_k-a_{n_k+1}.$$

Iterating from $K_0$ to any $K>K_0$,
$$r_K \;=\; r_{K_0}-\sum_{j=K_0}^{K-1} a_{n_j+1} \;=\; r_{K_0}-\sum_{i\,=\,n_{K_0}+1}^{\,n_{K}+1} a_i.$$
As $K\to\infty$ the index $n_K\to\infty$, so the sum on the right tends to $\sum_{i=n_{K_0}+1}^{\infty}a_i$, which is $+\infty$ because $\sum a_i=\infty$ (a tail of a divergent series of positive terms diverges). Thus $r_K\to -\infty$, contradicting $r_K\ge L/2>0$.

Hence $L=0$.

**Conclusion.** Since $r_k\to 0$ and $r_k=x-\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{n_j}$, we obtain
$$x \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_{n_k},$$
a subsequence sum. The argument uses only $a_i\to 0$, $\sum a_i=\infty$, and strict decrease (the last only to make "largest eligible term" unambiguous), so it applies to **every** sequence satisfying the hypotheses. Therefore every positive real number is representable as a subsequence sum. $\blacksquare$
